platforms.title: Why Dark Urine After a Workout Is Not Just Dehydration
platforms.meta_description: Cola-colored urine after intense exercise can signal rhabdomyolysis, a muscle breakdown that can injure the kidneys. Here's what the warning signs mean.
platforms.body_html:
Finishing an intense workout and noticing your urine has turned the color of cola or strong tea is easy to blame on not drinking enough water. But according to the CDC's National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health (NIOSH), dark urine described as "tea- or cola-colored" is one of the classic warning signs of rhabdomyolysis, a condition where muscle tissue breaks down and releases its contents into the bloodstream.

Why the Color Change Matters

When muscle cells are damaged by extreme exertion, they release a protein called myoglobin into the blood. The kidneys try to filter it out, and it is this myoglobin that turns urine dark brown or reddish. The CDC notes that alongside dark urine, people with rhabdomyolysis often report "muscle cramps, aches, or pains that are more severe than expected" and "feeling weak or tired, unable to complete tasks or finish a workout you were able to do previously." Importantly, symptoms may not appear until hours or even days after the muscle injury itself, so the connection to a specific workout is not always obvious right away.

What Actually Confirms the Diagnosis

Dark urine alone is not a reliable way to confirm rhabdomyolysis — research summarized by clinical references notes that visibly discolored urine only shows up in about 10 percent of cases, since myoglobin clears from the body quickly. The more dependable test is a blood test for creatine kinase (CK), an enzyme released by damaged muscle. Elevated CK can persist in the blood for days even after the urine returns to normal, which is why doctors are advised to check serial CK levels rather than relying on a urine dipstick test alone. If you have muscle pain and weakness after intense exercise and your provider does not mention a CK test, it is reasonable to ask for one directly.

3 Things to Do If You Suspect Rhabdomyolysis

  • Stop the activity and rehydrate — hydration supports kidney function while the muscle injury is assessed, though it will not resolve rhabdomyolysis on its own.
  • Seek medical care the same day — don't wait for the urine color to normalize before getting checked, since myoglobin clears faster than the underlying muscle damage.
  • Ask specifically for a creatine kinase blood test — this is the test that actually confirms muscle breakdown, not a urine strip.

The One Thing Worth Remembering

Heat and unaccustomed intensity are two of the biggest risk factors for exertional rhabdomyolysis, which is why cases tend to rise during summer training or a sudden return to a hard workout after time off. Ramping up intensity gradually, especially in hot weather, is the simplest way to avoid the muscle damage that leads to this warning sign in the first place. Athletes returning from an injury layoff or a long break from training are at particularly high risk, since the muscles have lost the conditioning that normally protects them from this kind of breakdown.
